# ocsync

[![CI](https://github.com/alv67/ocsync/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg?branch=develop)](https://github.com/alv67/ocsync/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue.svg)](LICENSE)
[![Project](https://img.shields.io/badge/project-roadmap-2f81f7)](https://github.com/users/alv67/projects/5)

Git-backed session sync for OpenCode V2.

> **Status: pre-alpha.** The core sync engine, CLI, and OpenCode server plugin are implemented and covered by unit and end-to-end tests. Child-session transfer and deletion propagation are still pending.

`ocsync` keeps OpenCode sessions in sync across machines without a resident sync service. Sessions are exported through the official OpenCode V2 HTTP API, stored as encrypted immutable blobs in a private Git repository, and imported on the other machine when needed.

## Why

OpenCode stores sessions in a local SQLite database. That is excellent for a single machine, but it means a session created on a laptop is invisible on a desktop. `ocsync` is built for people who use the same project from more than one computer and want to continue a session where they left it.

It is intentionally **not** a real-time collaboration layer. For that, connect multiple clients to the same OpenCode server. `ocsync` solves the offline and multi-server case.

## Design principles

- **Official API only.** Sessions are transferred with `session.export` and `session.import`. The OpenCode database is never modified directly.
- **No resident service.** The sync engine runs on demand, either from the CLI or from the OpenCode server plugin.
- **Conflict-preserving.** Two divergent edits to the same session are never silently merged or overwritten. Both branches are preserved.
- **Encrypted at rest.** Session blobs are encrypted before they reach Git.
- **No credential sync.** `ocsync` syncs sessions only. Provider credentials, auth files, and OpenCode configuration stay on each machine.
- **Boring transport.** A private Git repository is the source of truth, so the data is versioned and auditable.

## How it works

```text
OpenCode server ──export/import──> ocsync core ──> private Git repository
        ▲                                │
        └──────── plugin trigger ────────┘
```

- The **CLI** performs `status`, `push`, `pull`, and `sync`.
- The **server plugin** watches session events and invokes the CLI with a debounce. It runs inside the OpenCode server that is already running, so there is no extra daemon.
- Every session revision is an immutable encrypted blob. A per-device index points at the current head. Revisions form a hash chain, which lets `ocsync` distinguish a fast-forward from a real divergence.

See [docs/architecture.md](docs/architecture.md) for the full design.

## Requirements

- OpenCode V2 (`>= 2.0.29`)
- Git
- Bun 1.4+ for development and for building from source

## Install from source

```bash
git clone https://github.com/alv67/ocsync.git
cd ocsync
bun install
bun run build
bun link
ocsync --help
```

The npm package and prebuilt binaries are not published yet. The GitHub Project tracks the release work.

## Development

```bash
bun install
bun run check
bun run build
```

`bun run check` runs Biome, TypeScript, and the test suite.

### End-to-end check

With OpenCode V2 on `PATH`, run:

```bash
bash scripts/e2e.sh
```

The script starts two isolated OpenCode servers, creates a temporary session, pushes it from one server, pulls it into the other, and verifies the transcript. Set `KEEP_E2E=1` to keep the temporary directory for inspection.

The repository uses a two-branch model:

- `main` is release-only and protected.
- `develop` is the integration branch.
- Feature branches target `develop` through pull requests.

See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) and [docs/github-workflow.md](docs/github-workflow.md).

## [0.1.0] - 2026-10-26

### Added

- Initial project scaffold.
- Revision projection and parent-aware revision chain.
- Encrypted Git store with per-device indexes.
- OpenCode V2 HTTP client and session export/import support.
- Push/pull engine with fast-forward and conflict detection.
- OpenCode server plugin that triggers sync on session events.
- CLI commands: `init`, `status`, `push`, `pull`, `sync`, `key`, `doctor`.
- End-to-end two-server test script.
- Unit tests for revisions, crypto, configuration, project keys, Git storage, and the engine.
- CI workflow for Linux, macOS, and Windows.
- Architecture, GitHub workflow, and feasibility spike documentation.

### Fixed

- Pull no longer hides an unpushed local edit when the remote head is unchanged.
- Honor `--key-file` during `ocsync init`.

### Known limitations

- Child sessions are not synced yet.
- Remote deletions are not applied automatically.
- File snapshots and revert state are not transferred.
- Pulling an open-but-idle session needs end-to-end UI validation.

# Architecture

`ocsync` is a Git-backed transport for OpenCode V2 sessions. It is deliberately small: the OpenCode server remains the owner of sessions, and the data repository is an append-only store of encrypted revisions.

## Goals

- Continue a session on another machine without copying the OpenCode database.
- Preserve both sides when two machines edit the same session concurrently.
- Keep the transport auditable and versioned.
- Run no background service of its own.
- Never modify the OpenCode database directly.

## Non-goals

- Real-time collaboration on a single session.
- Merging two conversation transcripts into one linear history.
- Syncing provider credentials, authentication files, or OpenCode configuration.
- Syncing file snapshots or working-tree state. Code belongs in Git.
- Replacing the native remote-server workflow.

## Components

```text
┌──────────────────┐       export / import        ┌──────────────┐
│  OpenCode server │ <──────────────────────────> │ ocsync core  │
└──────────────────┘                              │              │
        ▲                                         │  revisions   │
        │ events                                  │  conflicts   │
        │                                         │  crypto      │
┌───────┴──────────┐                              └──────┬───────┘
│  server plugin   │                                     │
└──────────────────┘                              ┌──────▼───────┐
                                                  │  Git remote  │
                                                  │  (private)   │
                                                  └──────────────┘
```

- **Core** — revision projection, Git store, encryption, push/pull engine.
- **CLI** — the user-facing entry point and the code the plugin invokes.
- **Server plugin** — listens to session events and triggers a debounced sync. It runs inside the existing OpenCode server; it is not a separate daemon.
- **TUI plugin** — optional future surface for a status indicator and a manual sync command.

## Data model

Each session revision is an immutable encrypted blob plus a plaintext metadata record.

```text
revisions/<revision>.json
projects/<project-key>/sessions/<session-id>/<revision>.json.gz.enc
devices/<device-id>.json
```

### Revision record

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "sessionID": "ses_...",
  "project": "github.com/alv67/ocsync",
  "revision": "…64 hex chars…",
  "parentRevision": "…64 hex chars… or null",
  "deviceID": "dev_...",
  "createdAt": 1793000000000,
  "messageCount": 12,
  "lastMessageID": "msg_...",
  "blob": "projects/.../sessions/.../revision.json.gz.enc",
  "deleted": false
}
```

A revision identity is `sha256(parentRevision + ":" + contentRevision)`, not just the content hash. The parent is part of the identity because the same transcript can be reached from different history points.

### Device index

Every device writes only its own `devices/<device-id>.json`:

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "deviceID": "dev_...",
  "updatedAt": 1793000000000,
  "sessions": {
    "ses_...": {
      "revision": "…",
      "parentRevision": "…",
      "localRevision": "…",
      "deviceID": "dev_...",
      "createdAt": 1793000000000,
      "messageCount": 12,
      "lastMessageID": "msg_...",
      "blob": "…",
      "deleted": false
    }
  }
}
```

Because each device owns its index file, Git never needs to merge a session file. Revisions and blobs are immutable.

## Revision projection

The content revision is a deterministic hash of a projection of the exported session. The following are excluded because they differ between machines or do not survive import:

- `info.projectID`
- `info.location.directory`
- `info.time.updated`
- `info.time.viewed`
- `info.revert`
- `info.fork`

The import route sets `time.updated` to the import time and remaps the location, so comparing raw exports would produce false changes.

## Sync algorithm

### Push

1. Fetch and rebase the local data-repository clone.
2. Read the device index and all other device indexes.
3. For each root session in the project:
   - skip active sessions;
   - export the session;
   - skip it when its content revision matches `localRevision`;
   - compare the remote head with the local head:
     - remote is an ancestor of local → push a new revision;
     - local is an ancestor of remote → skip and pull first;
     - unrelated histories → report a conflict;
   - write an encrypted blob and revision record;
   - update the local device index.
4. Commit and push the index and immutable files.

### Pull

1. Fetch the data repository.
2. Collect every device's head for each session and reduce them to tips.
3. For each tip in this project:
   - skip active sessions;
   - skip child sessions for now;
   - if no local session exists, import the remote snapshot;
   - if local is unchanged and the remote tip descends from the local head, back up the local snapshot, delete it, and import the remote snapshot;
   - if local is unchanged and the local head descends from the remote tip, do nothing;
   - otherwise report a conflict.
4. Update the device index and push it.

### Conflicts

A conflict means the two sides have revisions that are not ancestors of one another. `ocsync` never picks a winner automatically. The current version reports the conflict and leaves both sides untouched. A future `resolve` command will import the remote branch under a new session ID, preserving both transcripts.

## Session replacement

OpenCode V2 has no in-place “update session” API. To replace a session with a newer revision, `ocsync`:

1. writes a plaintext local backup;
2. deletes the local session (the API cascades to child sessions);
3. imports the remote snapshot with the same session ID and the local project directory.

For that reason, a session with local child sessions is skipped until child-session sync is implemented.

## Encryption

- XChaCha20-Poly1305 with a 256-bit key.
- The blob format is `nonce (24 bytes) || ciphertext`.
- JSON is gzip-compressed before encryption.
- The key is stored at `~/.config/ocsync/key` with mode `0600`, or supplied through `OCSYNC_KEY` as base64.
- Git stores only ciphertext. The plaintext key never leaves the machine through `ocsync`.

Session transcripts can contain source code, shell output, and secrets. Treat the key as a secret. A private Git repository is still required, because metadata and commit history are visible.

## Server plugin

The plugin subscribes to the server event stream and filters by its location. It triggers pushes on:

- `session.execution.succeeded`
- `session.execution.failed`
- `session.execution.interrupted`
- `session.created`, `session.deleted`, `session.renamed`, `session.moved`
- `session.archived`, `session.unarchived`
- `session.idle`
- `session.status` with status `idle`

Pushes are debounced (`pushDebounceSec`, default 30 seconds). The plugin also pulls when the location opens and every `pullIntervalSec` seconds (default 120; set to `0` to disable).

The plugin invokes the `ocsync` binary as a subprocess. The server plugin context does not expose `session.export` or `session.import` directly, and subprocess execution was verified during the feasibility spike.

## Known limitations

- Child sessions (subagents) are not synced yet.
- Deletions are not propagated automatically.
- A session with local child sessions cannot be fast-forwarded safely and is skipped.
- File snapshots and revert history are not transferred.
- `fork` metadata and `revert` state are not preserved by the V2 import route.
- Pulling a session that is open but idle in a client can replace it; the engine only knows about active turns. This must be tested against TUI, web, and desktop clients.
- The desktop app must be verified to load server plugins from its configuration.

## Failure model

- The OpenCode database is never modified directly.
- Session blobs and revision records are immutable.
- Local snapshots are backed up before replacement.
- A failed import leaves the session deleted only if the backup step succeeded; the backup is written before any destructive call.
- A failed Git push can be retried; the local index is committed first.
- A missing or wrong key produces a decrypt error, not a partial import.

# GitHub workflow

`ocsync` uses a protected two-branch model.

## Branches

- **`main`** — releases only. Protected. Changes arrive through a pull request from `develop` or a `release/*` branch. No direct pushes, no force pushes, linear history.
- **`develop`** — integration branch. Features, fixes, documentation, and chores merge here through pull requests.
- **`feat/<scope>-<short-name>`** — new behavior.
- **`fix/<scope>-<short-name>`** — bug fix.
- **`docs/<short-name>`** — documentation only.
- **`chore/<short-name>`** — tooling, CI, dependencies.
- **`release/<version>`** — release stabilization, merged into `main` and back into `develop`.
- **`hotfix/<version>`** — emergency fix from `main`, merged into `main` and back into `develop`.

The repository bootstrap is the only direct commit to `main`. Every subsequent change follows the pull-request flow.

## Commits

Use Conventional Commits in English:

```text
feat(core): add revision ancestry
fix(plugin): debounce duplicate idle events
docs: describe the conflict model
chore(ci): add Windows to the matrix
```

Scopes: `core`, `cli`, `plugin`, `tui`, `crypto`, `docs`, `ci`.

## Pull requests

- Target `develop`, except `release/*` and `hotfix/*`.
- Use squash merge.
- CI must pass on Linux, macOS, and Windows.
- Include tests for behavior changes.
- Update documentation when public behavior changes.
- Do not commit secrets, keys, or session transcripts.
- All text is in English.
- Maintainers may self-merge a green PR; external contributions require a maintainer review.

## Issue triage

External issues do not become work items automatically. They must be evaluated.

1. New external issues receive the `needs-triage` label and enter the **Triage** stage of the project.
2. A maintainer checks reproducibility, scope, duplicates, and security impact.
3. The maintainer assigns `Kind` and `Area`.
4. The issue is either:
   - **accepted**: remove `needs-triage`, add `accepted`, set `Priority`, and move it to **Backlog** or **Ready**; or
   - **rejected**: close it with `duplicate`, `invalid`, or `wontfix`.
5. Only accepted issues are considered work items.

Security reports must not be filed as public issues. See [SECURITY.md](../SECURITY.md).

## Project fields

| Field    | Values                                               |
| -------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| Stage    | Triage, Backlog, Ready, In Progress, In Review, Done |
| Kind     | Bug, Feature, Chore, Docs, Spike, Security           |

| Area     | Core, CLI, Plugin, Crypto, Docs, CI                  |

## Labels

- Triage: `needs-triage`, `accepted`
- Type: `type: bug`, `type: feature`, `type: chore`, `type: docs`, `type: spike`, `type: security`
- Priority: `priority: p0` through `priority: p3`
- Area: `area: core`, `area: cli`, `area: plugin`, `area: crypto`, `area: docs`, `area: ci`
- Community: `good first issue`, `help wanted`, `dependencies`
- Resolution: `duplicate`, `invalid`, `wontfix`

## Releases

1. Create `release/<version>` from `develop`.
2. Update `package.json` and `CHANGELOG.md`.
3. Open a PR to `main`.
4. Merge after CI passes.
5. Tag the merge commit (`v<version>`) and create a GitHub Release.
6. Merge `main` back into `develop`.
7. Publish the package from the release commit.

`main` must always be releasable. Fix broken releases with a `hotfix/*` branch; do not force-push `main`.

# Feasibility spike — 2026-10-26

Environment:

- OpenCode `2.0.29`
- Bun `1.4.4`
- Ubuntu 26.04
- Git `2.53.0`

The spike validated the assumptions behind the architecture. It used isolated OpenCode servers with temporary databases and temporary project directories.

## Results

### Session export and import work through the official API

`GET /api/experimental/session/{id}/export` returns `{ info, messages }`. `POST /api/experimental/session/import` accepts the same object plus a target `location`.

Observed behavior:

- importing a session ID that already exists returns `409 Conflict`;
- the CLI `opencode session import` prints `Session already exists` but exits with code `0`, so the engine uses the HTTP API for reliable conflict detection;
- deleting the local session and importing again succeeds;
- the imported session keeps its ID and messages;
- `info.time.created` is preserved, while `info.time.updated` is set to the import time;
- `info.location.directory` is replaced with the target directory.

Conclusion: replacement is possible, but only through delete + re-import, and the revision model must not compare `time.updated` across machines.

### The active-session endpoint works

`GET /api/session/active` returns `{}` when no turn is running. The engine uses it to avoid touching sessions that are currently executing.

Open question: this endpoint does not report sessions that are merely open in a TUI or browser. Pulling an open-but-idle session needs an end-to-end UI test.

### Server plugins are a first-class extension point

A local plugin placed in `.opencode/plugins/<name>/index.ts` was discovered and loaded by OpenCode `2.0.29`. The loader also accepts the singular `.opencode/plugin` directory.

Verified in the running server:

- `setup(ctx)` ran;
- `Bun.spawn` worked and returned an exit code;
- `ctx.event.subscribe()` delivered live events;
- the cleanup function ran on plugin reload;
- the event stream includes events for every location on the server, so a plugin must filter by `event.location.directory`.

Relevant event types observed or defined by the V2 schema:

- `session.created`, `session.deleted`, `session.renamed`, `session.moved`, `session.archived`, `session.unarchived`
- `session.execution.started`, `session.execution.succeeded`, `session.execution.failed`, `session.execution.interrupted`
- `session.status` with `status.type` of `idle`, `busy`, or `retry`
- `session.idle` (deprecated, but still emitted)

The plugin context exposes `ctx.session.get`, `ctx.session.context`, and `ctx.session.remove`, but not `session.export` or `session.import`. The chosen integration is a thin plugin that spawns the `ocsync` CLI.

### Local service discovery works

The local OpenCode service registers itself at:

```text
~/.local/state/opencode/service.json
```

The file contains `url`, `password`, `pid`, and `version`. HTTP Basic authentication with username `opencode` (or `OPENCODE_SERVER_USERNAME`) and the registered password works against `/api/info`. `ocsync` uses this path for local operation and accepts `--server` plus `--password` for remote servers.

## Go/no-go

**Go.**

The official API supports the required transfer operations. The server plugin is a supported extension point and can spawn the CLI. No patch, fork, or database write is required.

The remaining risks are product risks, not platform blockers:

1. Pulling a session that is open but idle in a client.
2. Loading a server plugin in the Windows desktop app (expected, not yet tested).
3. Child sessions: the current MVP skips them to avoid deleting them when a parent is replaced.
4. Remote deletion handling.
5. Snapshot and revert state do not travel with a transcript.

These are tracked as separate work items in the GitHub Project.
